Maladaptive Strategies.value: Dates or anniversaries connected to the event
Going out at night or being outside after dark
Paying attention to or looking at my own body

Threat.value: I listen for sounds that might mean someone is entering my home
I frequently look behind me to check if someone is following me
Suddenly feeling or acting as if the stressful experience were actually happening again

Memory.value: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning
When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event.
When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened.

Negative Appraisals.value: My beliefs about how the world works have been completely destroyed
I am no longer capable of doing the things that defined me
Somebody else would have stopped the event from happening

issues.explanation: The trigger set is not clinically coherent for a single assault presentation as described. 'Shouting in Arabic' implies a very specific perpetrator/context cue, while 'fire or flames' suggests a qualitatively different trauma context that is not supported by the memory, appraisal, threat, or strategy items. This is hard to reconcile as one assault-based PTSD profile rather than merely heterogeneous triggers.

The threat item about monitoring for someone entering the home is weakly connected to the rest of the profile. Other threat items center on being followed and re-experiencing the assault, while the triggers and strategies point to external assault cues and body-related avoidance rather than a home-intrusion scenario. This makes the home-entry threat concern look like a mismatched threat context within the profile.

vignette: The assault occurred three months ago on a Tuesday evening outside a corner pharmacy on a busy commercial avenue. A silver motorcycle idled at the curb as a group of men stumbled from a nearby tavern. One of them grabbed her purse, and when she resisted, the encounter turned physical. The attacker’s breath carried the sharp, sweet tang of whiskey, and he shouted something in Arabic as he forced her against the brick facade. A second man revved his engine to cover her cries, and the high-pitched whine of the exhaust mixed with another voice yelling in Arabic. She managed to break free only when a neighbor’s dog began barking frantically. After that night, Clara’s life narrowed. She had come to believe that the ground beneath her feet was no longer reliable, that her foundational assumptions about how strangers move through shared public spaces had been completely destroyed. She knew somebody else would have stopped what happened to her, yet she found herself navigating a city that felt suddenly unguarded. What frightened her most was the quiet. She stopped walking without scanning the street behind her, her neck tense, eyes fixed on the rearview of passing cars to ensure no one was following. Inside her apartment on the second floor, she developed a habit of listening to the hallway long after her husband went to bed, her breath held tight, waiting for the specific scrape of a key in the lock or the heavy thud of a boot on the stairwell. Days bled into weeks, and the calendar became a landscape she refused to enter. She stopped marking dates on the wall, convinced that acknowledging the month would summon the memory. Going out after dark required a negotiation she could no longer make, so she stayed inside once the streetlights flickered on. When she needed to dress for grocery runs, she caught herself turning away from the hallway mirror, focusing only on her shoes. She could not bear to look at her own body, to trace the lines where her clothes had been pulled or where the brick had pressed into her skin. Instead, she relied on the sofa by the living room window, watching the avenue. The memories did not wait for permission. They arrived without warning when the wind shifted or a delivery truck passed. Sometimes, just as she folded laundry at the kitchen table, the smell of stale beer would rise in her nose, sharp and inescapable, and she would drop the basket. Other times, the sound of a motorcycle engine down the block sent her heart into a frantic rhythm against her ribs. She would press her palms to the windowsill, listening for the familiar rev of a two-stroke, certain the same mechanical scream was returning. During quiet dinners, she heard the shouts in her head, the Arabic syllables overlapping like static, and she would abruptly stand from the table. The memory would hit her so completely that she would suddenly feel the cold brick against her back and the weight of his hands again, acting as if the attack were occurring in real time. She tried to tell her husband how fractured her sense of safety had become, but words felt inadequate. The event had taken everything she believed about how people interact, and she no longer felt capable of returning to her part-time administrative work, or of walking to the bus stop like she used to. The things that had once defined her—her reliability, her steady pace, her ability to navigate crowds—felt like relics of a person who no longer existed. Now, at nineteen, Clara sits at the kitchen table with a referral slip and her husband’s key in her hand. She is unemployed, spending her days tracking the sounds of the neighborhood rather than engaging with them. What finally brought her to the clinic was not a single breakdown, but the slow, quiet realization that she could no longer step past her own front door without preparing for a threat that had already ended. She hopes the appointment will give her a way to quiet the monitoring, to stop flinching at the sight of a motorcycle, to find a version of herself that does not live in constant expectation of the next shout, the next smell, the next sudden return of the night.
